keyVerseText: And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam. Jair: called also, Iaare-ore-gim.2.Sam.21.19
rootMeaning: The root of לַחְמִי (Lachmîy) is לֶחֶם (lechem), which primarily means bread or food. This root conveys the fundamental idea of sustenance and nourishment, essential for life. The name לַחְמִי literally means "my bread," reflecting a personal or possessive form of this vital provision. This literal sense enriches the understanding of the word beyond a mere proper name, linking it to the concept of sustenance and life-giving provision.
usageInScripture: The term לַחְמִי appears only once in Scripture, specifically as a proper name referring to an individual, Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite. The translation consistently renders it as 'Lahmi,' preserving its identity as a person rather than a common noun. This singular usage highlights the name's unique role and its connection to the narrative of conflict with the Philistines, rather than a broader lexical range.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding לַחְמִי as 'my bread' invites reflection on God as the ultimate provider and sustainer of life, echoing the deeper biblical theme of God as the Bread of Life. Although the name here identifies a Philistine warrior, its root reminds believers of the sustenance found in God alone. This contrast underscores the spiritual nourishment found in Christ, who satisfies the soul beyond physical provision. Recognizing the personal and possessive nature of the name also points to the intimate relationship God desires with His people, offering Himself as their true bread and sustenance.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Chronicles 20:5 recounts that Elhanan, son of Jair, killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath, emphasizing the defeat of Israel's enemies. The use of לַחְמִי here identifies a specific adversary linked to Goliath, highlighting the reality of spiritual and physical battles faced by God's people. The name's meaning, 'my bread,' subtly contrasts the enemy's reliance on earthly strength with the believer's dependence on divine provision and victory through God.
